transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-02
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 50 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Carter (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Alex Chen (Parallax Eng Lead), Priya Singh (Parallax PM), Samir Patel (Parallax DevOps)

Summary:
Quickwalk onboarding for Parallax AI: SDK install (Python + TS), auth patterns (sandbox keys, SSO, K M S notes), environment and CI best practices, and next steps to start a short PoC. Quick demo of Console, streaming responses, and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization.

Topics covered:
- SDK quickstart (pip/npm) and .env/CI secrets
- Sandbox provisioning and short-lived API keys
- SSO/SAML + RBAC and KMS/HSM integration notes
- Console walkthrough: token usage, model selection, rollouts, Optimize tips
- PoC scope and performance targets

Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Jamie from Redwood, this is Luis our solutions engineer. How are you folks?
[00:07] Alex: Good, thanks. We have Priya and Samir on, we're excited to get hands on.
[00:12] Jamie: Awesome. So quick agenda: we want to show the SDK onramp, auth and sandbox, a quick Console tour, and then call out a recommended PoC. Any additions?
[00:20] Priya: That's great, maybe emphasize the SSO and security bit — compliance is our main blocker.
[00:25] Luis: Yep totally, we'll go into SOC2, KMS and RBAC. Also show how to rotate keys via the API.
[00:32] Samir: And infra-wise we care about VPC/private deployment options and what latencies look like — so please keep that in mind.
[00:38] Luis: Will do. Alright, starting SDK quickstart — I have a tiny terminal demo. For Python: pip install redwood-sdk, then set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your .env or CI secrets. For TypeScript: npm i @redwood/inference and using process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY or dotenv file.
[00:55] Alex: Are there official typed examples for both? We prefer TS for our front-end services.
[01:00] Luis: Yes, we maintain examples in the repo. I'll drop the link after the call. They include streaming, function calling, and websocket examples.
[01:08] Priya: When you say streaming, is that server-sent events or websockets?
[01:12] Luis: We support SSE streaming via the REST SDK and also gRPC/websocket for lower-latency bi-directional. For most quickstarts SSE is easiest.
[01:21] Jamie: I'll put the SDK sample repo link in the notes: https://redwood.example.com/repos/onramp-parallax (shared).
[01:28] Alex: Cool. On auth — we want SSO, scoping, and rotate keys automatically. How do you recommend?
[01:34] Luis: Two patterns. For dev/sandbox: short-lived API keys provisioned per user or team, rotated by an infra job. For production: use SSO via SAML/SCIM to manage RBAC and service accounts. Keys should be wrapped by your KMS; Redwood accepts customer-managed keys via our KMS/HSM integration or we can integrate with cloud KMS.
[01:50] Samir: When you say "wrap" the keys, do you mean envelope encryption on our end?
[01:55] Luis: Right — you can bring-your-own-key (BYOK) so the actual model tokens are encrypted under your KMS key. For the control plane we support integrating with AWS KMS and GCP KMS; HSM is an add-on.
[02:04] Priya: Any compliance docs for this?
[02:07] Jamie: Yes, we'll send SOC2 + the KMS integration playbook. It's in the security pack.
[02:11] Alex: Great. Ok, environment and CI: how do you recommend we store keys for ephemeral test runs?
[02:16] Luis: Use ephemeral sandbox keys with short TTLs. In CI, keep them in secrets manager (GitHub Actions secrets, or Hashi Vault). We recommend never committing .env files; use dotenv during local dev. We have an example GitHub Actions workflow in the repo that fetches a short-lived key via an internal infra endpoint.
[02:33] Alex: Perfect. Can you demo the Console quickly? We want to see model selection and cost insights.
[02:38] Jamie: Yup — switching screens.. (pause, slight typing) Console shows model catalog, per-model latency and cost estimates, token-level breakdowns, and per-route dashboards. You can pin a model version and create a canary rollout. If traffic spikes we have automatic fallback to compatible model variants to maintain throughput.
[02:57] Priya: Is observability data available at token-level? We need to tie regressions to specific prompts.
[03:02] Luis: Yes, you can tie eval sets to alerts — Redwood Optimize can watch a prompt set and fire regressions. We also export traces and logs to your SIEM if you want.
[03:12] Alex: Any ETA on private deployments? We might need an on-prem option for a later phase.
[03:16] Jamie: We support VPC and on-prem — Private deployment has a different contract and deployment runway. For PoC, starting hosted with a dedicated pool is faster, then transition to Private if needed.
[03:26] Samir: Latency numbers — do you have ballpark per-token latencies for gen models on Dedicated?
[03:30] Luis: Ballpark: a small-to-medium open decoder on a modern GPU is in the ~40-120ms per token range depending on prompt length and batching. For large fanout workloads we recommend quantization + batching to reduce cost; Optimize will recommend specific quant profiles. These are approximate — we should run benchmarks with your payloads.
[03:46] Alex: Ok we'll share a sample corpus.
[03:48] Priya: PoC scope — we want a small user-facing feature that has a 2-week runway.
[03:53] Jamie: Recommended PoC: 2-week sandbox, up to 10k tokens/day, use Python and TS SDKs for back-end + front-end streaming. We'll provision a dedicated sandbox key, set up a basic alert for latency and quality drift, and run a small Optimize pass on quantization suggestions.
[04:09] Samir: How do we measure quality drift?
[04:12] Luis: Tie eval prompts with expected outputs; Optimize will score outputs against gold labels and raise alerts if metrics fall below a threshold. Also you can export tokens to S3 or your internal storage for offline review.
[04:24] Alex: Any blockers we should expect around procurement or network?
[04:27] Jamie: Procurement is usually the longer pole for Private — for hosted we have a quick TOS and an enterprise contract for dedicated pools. On networking, VPC peering and egress rules are discussed during Private onboarding. We'll include a network checklist.
[04:41] Priya: About pricing — can you share a sample estimate for the PoC?
[04:44] Jamie: Yes I'll send a short pricing sheet: hosted per-token rates + optional dedicated monthly commit. For the PoC we can do a usage-based short term credit and then convert if you like the results.
[04:53] Alex: Cool. A couple of technical clarifications: can we run local inference for edge devices, or must it go through Redwood?
[05:00] Luis: Redwood focuses on centralized inference; we do support private on-prem packages but not lightweight edge SDKs. If you need edge-run models, you'll need a separate packaging route.
[05:09] Samir: Understood. Final question — any known limitations with function calling / structured outputs?
[05:14] Luis: Function calling works and we support structured JSON outputs, but sometimes the transcriber (uh, generator) can vary; we recommend schema validation and a small post-processor. Also watch tokenization edge cases for long sequences.
[05:26] Jamie: Alright let's recap next steps — we'll provide security docs, a sandbox key, sample repos and CI examples, and schedule a technical deep dive.
[05:33] Alex: Sounds good. Anything else?
[05:35] Priya: No, that's it. Thanks.
[05:36] Jamie: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the pack and links.

Shared artifacts/links mentioned:
- SDK sample repo: https://redwood.example.com/repos/onramp-parallax
- Security pack (SOC2 + KMS playbook): will be emailed by Jamie
- Quick pricing sheet: will be attached to follow-up email

End of transcript.
